rd-school-c8-english.ch01-best-christmas.title: The Best Christmas Present in the World — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch01-best-christmas.subtitle: A secret drawer, a 1914 letter from the trenches, and a 101-year-old woman waiting for her Jim

sections.h: Before you read: a truce in the middle of a war
sections.md:
What if, in the middle of a terrible war, soldiers on both sides simply stopped fighting for a day — and played football?

That really happened. **World War I** began in 1914 between the Allies (including Britain and France) and the Central Powers (including Germany). Along the **Western Front** in France and Belgium, soldiers lived in muddy **trenches** facing each other across a strip of shell-torn land called **no man's land**. On **Christmas Eve and Christmas Day 1914**, in many places along the line, British and German soldiers sang carols, came out of their trenches, shook hands, exchanged small gifts and in some places played informal football. It is remembered as the **Christmas Truce**. The war itself went on until 1918 and millions died.

The story in this chapter, by the British author **Michael Morpurgo** (born 1943), uses this true event as its heart. Because the author is living, his text is protected by copyright. This companion therefore gives a **complete retelling in our own words**, explains each part, and helps you prepare for exams. Read the original in your NCERT book *Honeydew* (free on ncert.nic.in).

sections.h: Scene 1: the desk in the junk shop
sections.md:
The narrator, who lives in England, spots an old **roll-top desk** in a junk shop in Bridport. It is made of oak and is very old, probably from the early 1900s, but it has been badly burnt and one leg is broken. The shopkeeper says it was damaged in a fire and needs a lot of work. The narrator, who enjoys restoring furniture, buys it cheaply anyway, thinking of it as a project.

At home he works on it. The roll-top is stuck, so he takes it off and finds the inside has drawers and pigeon-holes. One drawer will not open at all. When he finally gets it open — prising it, gently — he discovers a hidden **small drawer**, and inside, a small black **tin box**. Taped to the lid is a note in shaky handwriting saying that this was Jim's last letter, received on 26 January 1915, and that it should be buried with the writer when she dies. Inside the box is the letter.

**Meaning:** The opening is quiet and ordinary — a man and an old piece of furniture. The secret drawer is like a door into history. The note tells us someone treasured this letter so much she wanted it buried with her.

check.q: Where does the narrator find the letter?
options: In a secret drawer of a roll-top desk, in a tin box
check.why: He found a tin box in a hidden drawer of the damaged roll-top desk he bought.

sections.h: Scene 2: Jim's letter — Christmas in the trenches
sections.md:
The letter is dated **26 December 1914** and is written by **Jim Macpherson**, a British soldier (a captain), to his wife **Connie**. He tells her about the most extraordinary day of his life — Christmas Day.

It was a crisp, frosty morning. Jim was in his trench. Suddenly, from the German trenches, someone called out a Christmas greeting in English. Then the Germans began to sing a carol, and the British replied with one of their own. Soon a German officer climbed out of the trench waving a white flag, and walked into no man's land. Jim decided to go out too. Others followed on both sides.

The German officer introduced himself as **Hans Wolf** from **Düsseldorf**... (the story places him from a city in Germany where he plays the cello in an orchestra; check your book for the exact detail). He spoke good English. He was a musician and had a wife and a young daughter. The two men talked as if they had always been friends. Soldiers exchanged gifts — the Germans had **schnapps and sausages**; the British had **chocolate, biscuits and tea**. Hans and Jim agreed how silly the war was.

Then someone produced a football, and soon a game began, with coats as goalposts. The narrator of the letter comments that the Germans won 2–1 — and jokes that the Germans' goal was offside. The soldiers then returned to their trenches. Hans and Jim shook hands and wished each other well, and Jim notes that by evening the guns started again. He writes sadly that the war would be decided not by politicians but by ordinary men like them — and that if they had been left to it, there would be no war at all, because people who are not enemies do not want to kill each other.

Jim ends with longing: he hopes the war will be over soon and that he will come home to Connie. He imagines himself walking up to their house and being with her again.

**Meaning:** This is the emotional centre. The enemy is shown as human: a musician, a husband, a father. The football match symbolises shared humanity. The letter's hope of an early homecoming makes the reader fear what happened next.

check.q: What did the soldiers do together on Christmas Day?
options: Exchanged gifts, talked and played football
check.why: They met in no man's land, shared food and drink, talked and played a football match.

sections.h: A note on details to check in your textbook
sections.md:
Some small details in retellings get muddled, so verify them against your NCERT book before an exam: the German officer's **home city** (the story names a German city and says he played in an orchestra), what exactly the soldiers exchanged, and the **football score** as Jim reports it. In exams, you will be asked mostly about **events, characters, themes and the ending**, which are summarised accurately here.

What matters most:
- **Jim Macpherson** writes the letter to **Connie** on 26 December 1914.
- **Hans Wolf** is the German officer he befriends.
- They share food, drink, talk and football in no man's land.
- Both sides return to fighting.
- Jim dreams of coming home.

check.q: To whom is Jim's letter addressed?
check.why: Jim writes to his beloved wife Connie.

sections.md:
The narrator is deeply moved. He realises that the desk must have belonged to Connie, and that the note on the box meant Jim never came home. He wants to return the letter to her family or to Connie herself, even though she would be very old.

He goes back to the junk shop. The owner tells him the desk came from a house that had caught fire — the house of an old lady, which is how the desk got burnt. With this clue he finds out that **Connie Macpherson** is alive. She is **101 years old** and lives in a nursing home, **Burlington House**, near Bridport, after her own house was damaged by fire.

The narrator goes to the nursing home with the letter.

check.q: How old is Connie when the narrator finds her?
check.why: Connie Macpherson is 101 years old and lives in a nursing home.

sections.md:
A nurse leads the narrator to Connie's room. She is sitting in a rocking chair with a smile, very old and frail. When the narrator gives her the tin box, she recognises it immediately. She is overjoyed to have it back after losing it in the fire.

Then she looks at the narrator and calls him **Jim**. She believes he is her husband, come home at last, just as he promised in his letter. She tells him she knew he would come back, and that he looks just the same as ever. She speaks of the desk, and says the letter is the one she kept. The narrator does not correct her. He understands that the kindest thing is to let her joy remain.

Connie says that it is the **best Christmas present in the world** — Jim coming home for Christmas, just as he promised. She holds his hand, and they sit together talking about the old days.

**Meaning:** The ending is both happy and heartbreaking. For Connie, the present is Jim's return; for the reader, it is a reminder that Jim died in the war and she waited all her life. The narrator's silence is an act of compassion.

sections.md:
**Characters**
- **The narrator:** curious, sensitive and kind. He restores old furniture, is touched by the letter, takes trouble to find Connie, and protects her happiness.
- **Jim Macpherson:** a brave, humane British soldier; loving husband; sees the futility of war and the humanity of the enemy.
- **Connie Macpherson:** Jim's wife; faithful for a lifetime; now 101 and confused by age, she lives with the hope that Jim will return.
- **Hans Wolf:** a German officer and musician; friendly, educated, a family man — the 'enemy' who is just like Jim.

**Themes**
1. **Futility of war:** ordinary soldiers have no quarrel with each other.
2. **Shared humanity:** carols, gifts and football unite enemies.
3. **Love and loyalty:** Connie kept Jim's letter close all her life.
4. **Memory and history:** an old desk carries a story across 80+ years.
5. **Kindness:** the narrator's quiet compassion.

**Title:** The 'present' is Jim's homecoming in Connie's eyes. Ironically, the reader knows the truth, which makes the title poignant.

**Language notes:** The story uses a **frame narrative** — a present-day story (narrator) holds an inner story (letter). Words to know: *roll-top desk, trenches, no man's land, truce, schnapps, offside, nursing home*.

check.q: The story's structure of a present-day story containing a letter is called a:
check.why: An outer narrative frames an inner narrative, here the letter from 1914.

sections.h: The ending: what is really happening?
sections.md:
The most discussed question about this story is its last scene. Connie Macpherson is a very old woman living in a nursing home in Bridport. When the narrator brings her the letter, she mistakes **him** for her husband **Jim**, who wrote it in 1914 and promised to come home. She says the desk was the best Christmas present.

What do we, the readers, know that Connie does not?
- The letter was written on Christmas Day **1914**; the narrator visits her many decades later.
- Jim was a young captain at the front. The story strongly suggests he **never came home** — he may have died in the war. The letter lay hidden in a secret drawer of the roll-top desk.
- Connie, now over a hundred and confused with age, believes Jim has finally returned.

The narrator does not correct her. Why? Because the truth would only cause pain, while letting her believe brings her joy at Christmas. This is an act of **kindness and compassion**. The 'best Christmas present' is therefore double: the desk Jim once gave her, and the 'return' of Jim she feels now.

**Exam tip:** When asked 'Do you think Jim came home?', give a reasoned answer and check the clues in your textbook — the hidden letter, Connie living alone in a home, and her confusion. Most readers conclude he did not.

check.q: Why does the narrator not tell Connie he is not Jim?
options: He does not want to hurt her and lets her enjoy her happiness
check.why: His silence is a compassionate choice that lets a lonely old woman believe her husband has come home.

sections.md:
- **The narrator** — curious, honest and deeply kind. He buys a damaged desk, finds the letter, and instead of keeping it, takes trouble to find its owner.
- **Jim Macpherson** — a young British captain in 1914; loving, hopeful and fair-minded. He sees the German soldiers as human beings like himself, and dreams that quarrels between nations could be settled by a game of football instead of fighting.
- **Hans Wolf** — the German officer Jim talks with during the truce; friendly and courteous. Their talk about home, family and music shows that the 'enemy' is also an ordinary person with dreams. (Check your textbook for the details he shares about his home town and work.)
- **Connie** — Jim's wife; her love has stayed true through a lifetime of waiting.

**Themes to remember:** the futility of war; common humanity on both sides; love and hope; the power of a letter to cross time.

check.q: What does Jim's friendship with Hans Wolf mainly show?
options: Soldiers on both sides were ordinary people with similar hopes
check.why: Their friendly talk during the truce reveals the shared humanity that war hides.

sections.md:
**Working with the text** asks you to recall facts: what the narrator found in the desk; who wrote the letter and to whom; why the soldiers stopped fighting on Christmas; what game they played; why Connie thinks the narrator is Jim.

**Working with language** includes:
- **Past perfect tense** — for an action completed before another past action: *By the time I reached the home, Connie had gone to sleep.* Practise combining two past events with *had* + past participle.
- **Reported speech** of letter lines — change tense and pronouns: Jim *wrote that he had spent the day talking with the enemy*.
- **Expressions** from the story such as *to come across* (find by chance) and *in a sorry state* (badly damaged).

**Speaking/writing tasks:** imagine you are Hans Wolf and write a letter home about the same Christmas day; or write a diary entry as the narrator after visiting Connie. Keep the tone warm and personal, and use details from the story.

**Official text:** read the full story free in *Honeydew* (Class 8) on ncert.nic.in.

rd-school-c8-english.ch02-tsunami.title: The Tsunami — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch02-tsunami.subtitle: 26 December 2004: courage, loss, a girl's geography lesson and animals that sensed the wave

sections.h: The morning the sea pulled back
sections.md:
Imagine standing on a beach and watching the sea suddenly **retreat** — far beyond the lowest tide you have ever seen. Fish flap on the wet sand. Boats tilt in the mud. People walk out, curious. Minutes later, a wall of water returns.

This happened on the morning of **26 December 2004**. A massive **earthquake** (magnitude about 9.1) struck under the Indian Ocean off the coast of **Sumatra, Indonesia**. It shifted the sea floor and set off a series of giant waves — a **tsunami** (a Japanese word meaning "harbour wave"). The waves struck the coasts of **Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand** and many other countries. In India, the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**, Tamil Nadu (including Nagapattinam), Kerala and Andhra Pradesh were badly affected. Around 2.3 lakh people died across the region.

The NCERT chapter *The Tsunami* (in *Honeydew*) is a set of **true accounts** compiled from news reports. Because it is an NCERT-prepared text, this companion retells each account in our own words and explains it; read the original free on ncert.nic.in. Small details (exact names, ages, places) should be checked against your textbook before exams.

check.why: A huge earthquake under the Indian Ocean near Sumatra displaced the sea floor and set off the waves.

sections.md:
On **Katchal**, one of the Nicobar Islands, **Ignesious** worked as a manager in a cooperative society. Early that morning the earthquake shook the island. When it stopped, his wife noticed something terrifying: the sea was rising and coming towards them. Ignesious tried to get his family to safety. He grabbed two of his children and his wife grabbed the other.

The giant waves struck. Ignesious lost his **wife, two of his children, his father-in-law and brother-in-law** to the sea (check the exact family members in your textbook). Some of his family survived because they ran to higher ground. The account is told simply, almost like a news report, which makes the loss more painful.

**Meaning:** The wave arrived within minutes of the quake. Families had almost no time. The story shows the speed and suddenness of the disaster and the grief of survivors.

check.q: What warning did Ignesious's wife notice after the earthquake?
check.why: She saw the sea rising and approaching, the sign of the tsunami.

sections.h: Account 2: a policeman's sacrifice and a girl who floated
sections.md:
Also on Katchal lived **Sanjeev**, a policeman. When the wave struck, he managed to save himself — but he heard the cries of a woman being swept away, the wife of a guest house worker. He jumped into the water to save her. Neither of them survived. His own wife and children were also lost. His selfless act shows **courage and humanity** in the face of death.

Another account tells of **Meghna**, a young girl (13) from **Car Nicobar** (check your book). The wave washed away her parents and swept her out to sea. She survived by clinging to a **piece of wooden debris** and floating for **two days**. Finally, she was washed back towards the shore and rescued. Her story is about **endurance and survival against odds**.

A third account tells of **Almas Javed**, a ten-year-old girl in **Port Blair**. Her father ran the family's business and her mother was from a family in Nicobar. On that morning they were... the wave struck as the family was at the seaside; her parents and grandparents were lost. Almas clung to a piece of wood and survived, though she was badly hurt. She could not speak about her experience for days (check details in your book).

**Meaning:** These short stories show different faces of the disaster: sacrifice (Sanjeev), survival (Meghna) and the trauma of children who lost everything (Almas).

check.q: Why is Sanjeev remembered?
options: He tried to rescue a drowning woman and lost his life
check.why: Sanjeev jumped back into the water to save a woman being swept away and died trying.

sections.h: Account 3: Tilly Smith on a Thai beach
sections.md:
In **Thailand**, a ten-year-old British schoolgirl named **Tilly Smith** was holidaying with her parents and younger sister on **Maikhao beach** in **Phuket**. The morning seemed ordinary. Then Tilly noticed that the water was behaving strangely: it was **bubbling** and **frothing**, and the tide **suddenly went out** far from the shore.

Tilly remembered her **geography lesson** at school in England just two weeks earlier, where her teacher had explained earthquakes and how they can cause tsunamis — and that the sea going out suddenly and frothing is a warning. She told her mother that a tsunami was coming. At first her mother did not understand the word. Tilly kept insisting; her parents took her seriously.

Their family alerted others, and the beach and a nearby hotel were **evacuated**. The beach was one of the few in Phuket where **no one was killed or seriously hurt**. Tilly's quick thinking saved around a hundred lives (exact figure: see your book).

**Meaning:** Knowledge from a classroom saved lives. It shows why learning about natural disasters — and listening to children — matters.

sections.md:
One of the most surprising parts of the chapter is about **animals**. Many people noticed that animals seemed to sense the tsunami before humans did.

- In **Sri Lanka**, at **Yala National Park**, the waves flooded a big part of the coast, killing many people (including visitors) — yet **very few dead animals** were found. Elephants, leopards, deer and other animals seemed to have moved to **higher ground** before the waves arrived.
- Some witnesses reported **elephants** screaming and running away from the beach.
- **Dogs** refused to go for their usual walks on the beach; some owners followed their dogs to safety.
- Flamingos left their low-lying breeding areas.

Why? Scientists suggest that animals may have a **sixth sense** for danger, or may hear or feel low-frequency vibrations (from the earthquake and waves) that humans cannot. The chapter presents this as a fascinating possibility rather than a proven fact.

**Meaning:** Nature has warning systems we are still learning from; paying attention to animal behaviour may help.

check.q: What was surprising at Yala National Park?
options: Very few dead animals were found
check.why: Animals seemed to move to higher ground in time, so very few animal deaths were found.

sections.h: Understanding the chapter: themes and language
sections.md:
**Structure.** The chapter is not one story but a **collection of real accounts**, like a news feature. Each is short, factual and moving. Together they show the scale of the tragedy across countries.

**Themes**
1. **Power of nature:** a disaster that crossed an entire ocean in hours.
2. **Human courage and sacrifice:** Sanjeev's rescue attempt.
3. **Survival and hope:** Meghna and Almas cling on and survive.
4. **Knowledge saves lives:** Tilly's lesson.
5. **Animal instinct:** creatures sensing danger.
6. **Loss and grief:** families torn apart, especially in the Nicobar Islands.

**What causes a tsunami? (science link).** A large undersea earthquake suddenly lifts or drops the sea floor. The whole column of water above moves, creating waves that spread outward in all directions. In deep ocean the waves are fast (as fast as a jet plane, around 700–800 km/h) but low; near the shore they slow down and pile up into tall walls of water. The sea often **draws back** first.

**Safety:** If you feel a strong earthquake near the coast or see the sea retreat suddenly, move **immediately to high ground** or inland; do not go to look. After the 2004 disaster, India set up a **tsunami warning centre** at INCOIS, Hyderabad (2007).

**Vocabulary:** *tsunami, debris, evacuate, trauma, aftershock, relief camp, instinct, magnitude*.

check.q: If the sea suddenly retreats far from the shore, you should:
check.why: A sudden retreat can signal an approaching tsunami, so moving inland and uphill saves lives.

sections.h: Before you read: what is a tsunami?
sections.md:
*Tsunami* is a Japanese word meaning 'harbour wave'. It is a series of very long, powerful waves caused when a large volume of sea water is suddenly pushed up or down — most often by an **undersea earthquake**, sometimes by an underwater landslide or volcanic eruption.

On **26 December 2004**, a huge earthquake (about magnitude 9.1) struck under the sea off the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia. The sea floor jerked upward along a long crack, lifting the water above it. Waves raced across the Indian Ocean at the speed of a jet plane — hundreds of kilometres per hour in deep water. In deep water they were low and hard to notice; as they reached shallow coasts they slowed down, piled up and rose into walls of water several metres high.

The tsunami struck Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Puducherry, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands), Thailand, the Maldives and even the coast of East Africa. More than two lakh people lost their lives across the region, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#e3f2fd'/><rect x='0' y='120' width='460' height='120' fill='#64b5f6'/><polygon points='460,240 600,150 600,280 460,280' fill='#d7ccc8'/><rect x='0' y='240' width='600' height='40' fill='#8d6e63'/><rect x='60' y='225' width='80' height='15' fill='#5d4037'><animate attributeName='y' values='240;225;225' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><path d='M0 120 Q30 110 60 120' fill='none' stroke='#0d47a1' stroke-width='5'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='60 0;400 -40' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='40' y='265' fill='#fff'>Sea floor lifts in earthquake</text><text x='200' y='100'>Wave grows taller in shallow water →</text><text x='500' y='140'>Coast</text></g></svg>

check.q: Why does a tsunami grow taller near the coast?
options: It slows in shallow water and the water piles up
check.why: As the wave enters shallow water it slows down, so the water behind piles up and the wave height increases.

sections.md:
The chapter shows that knowledge saved lives. Tilly Smith remembered her geography lesson; the animals sensed danger and fled to higher ground. Here are the natural warnings scientists describe:

1. **Strong shaking** near the coast — if you feel an earthquake on a beach, move inland and uphill at once.
2. **The sea suddenly drawing back**, exposing the sea bed, fish and rocks — the trough of the wave arriving first.
3. **Frothing, bubbling water** and an unusual roar from the sea.

What to do: do not go to look at the exposed sea floor; move quickly to high ground or the upper floors of a strong building; stay away until officials say it is safe, because tsunamis come in several waves and the later ones can be bigger.

**Did you know?** After 2004, India set up the **Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre** at INCOIS, Hyderabad (2007), which watches the Indian Ocean and issues alerts to coastal states.

check.q: If the sea suddenly pulls back from a beach, what should you do?
check.why: A sudden retreat of the sea is a warning that a tsunami wave may follow within minutes.

sections.h: Exercise topics: working with the text and language
sections.md:
**Working with the text** asks you to explain, from the accounts in the chapter:
- How the family of Ignesious in Katchal was affected, and how his son-in-law and his family were saved.
- How the police officer at Katchal lost his family while helping others.
- How Meghna and Almas survived, and what the experience was like for each.
- What Tilly Smith had learnt in school, and how she used it to warn her parents and others on the beach in Thailand.
- How animals at Yala National Park in Sri Lanka appear to have escaped — and why scientists think animals may sense vibrations or changes in air pressure.

**Working with language:**
- **Dictionary skills** — the exercise trains you to find the meaning of words in context and identify parts of speech. Look up words such as *tremor*, *debris*, *evacuate* and *casualty*.
- **Using words in sentences** — e.g. *The villagers were evacuated before the cyclone hit.*
- **Speaking and writing** — prepare a short talk on what to do in a natural disaster, or write a news report on the tsunami using headings, place, date and quotes from survivors (invented by you).

**Official text:** read the full chapter free in *Honeydew* (Class 8) on ncert.nic.in.
keyTerms: Tsunami — 'harbour wave'; giant sea waves from an undersea disturbance
Epicentre — point on the surface above an earthquake's origin
Evacuate — move people from danger to safety
Debris — broken pieces left after destruction

summary: Tsunami is Japanese for 'harbour wave'.
The 2004 tsunami was caused by a huge undersea earthquake off Sumatra on 26 December.
Waves travel very fast in deep water and grow tall near the coast.
It affected India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Indonesia, the Maldives and more.
Warning signs: shaking, sea drawing back, frothing water and a roar.
Move to high ground; tsunamis come in several waves.
Tilly Smith's lesson shows the value of knowledge.
Animals may sense vibrations and flee early.
India set up a Tsunami Early Warning Centre in Hyderabad in 2007.
practice: What is a tsunami and what causes it?
How did Tilly Smith save lives?
Narrate the experience of either Meghna or Almas in your own words.
Why do some people believe animals have a sixth sense? What do scientists say?
List three natural warning signs of a tsunami.
Write a news report on the 2004 tsunami in about 120 words.
Find the meaning and part of speech of: tremor, debris, evacuate.
What lessons can coastal communities learn from the 2004 tsunami?

rd-school-c8-english.ch03-glimpses-of-th.title: Glimpses of the Past — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch03-glimpses-of-th.subtitle: A hundred years in pictures: from Plassey to the great revolt of 1857

sections.h: A history told like a comic book
sections.md:
Imagine a hundred years of history squeezed into a set of drawings with speech bubbles. That is exactly what this chapter is: a **picture-story** (a short graphic novel) covering roughly **1757 to 1857** — the century in which the **East India Company**, a British trading company, turned itself into the ruler of much of India, and at the end of which Indian soldiers, peasants and princes rose against it.

The chapter moves frame by frame, and each frame carries one historical idea:

1. India divided among quarrelling rulers, while the Company watches.
2. Company officers taking advantage of the quarrels.
3. Farmers crushed by taxes; landlords and moneylenders squeezing them.
4. Indian industry ruined by British trade laws.
5. Social evils, and the reformer **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**.
6. British laws that hurt Indian rulers, soldiers and religious feelings.
7. Growing anger among sepoys, ending in the **Revolt of 1857**.

Because the chapter is mostly pictures, many students rush through it in five minutes. Don't! This companion slows down and retells each scene in our own words, explains the speech bubbles' meaning, and gives you the exam answers.

**Did you know?** You meet the same events in your Class 8 History book (*Our Pasts – III*): 'From Trade to Territory', 'Ruling the Countryside' and 'When People Rebel'. Reading both together makes each easier.

check.q: What period does 'Glimpses of the Past' mainly cover?
check.why: The picture-story traces events from the Plassey era to the Revolt of 1857.

sections.h: Scene 1–2: A divided land and a clever company
sections.md:
The story opens in the 1700s. The great **Mughal empire** has weakened. India is a patchwork of kingdoms, nawabs and chiefs who distrust one another. The pictures show rulers busy with pleasure and intrigue, not noticing the real danger.

The East India Company had come only to trade, but it kept its own army. When one ruler asked for help against a rival, the Company agreed — for a price: money, land, or the right to collect taxes. Soon the 'helper' controlled the helped. Frame after frame shows British officers smiling as Indian princes quarrel.

At **Plassey (1757)** in Bengal, the Company defeated Nawab **Siraj-ud-daulah**, helped by traitors in his own court. In **1765** it gained the *Diwani* — the right to collect revenue in Bengal. Over the next century wars, treaties and later the **Doctrine of Lapse** (taking over a state if its ruler died without a natural male heir) gave the Company most of India.

The frames also show a common Indian saying of the time: people thought the foreigners had come only to trade and would never become rulers. That complacency was costly.

**Lesson of the scene:** disunity among Indians made it easy for a small outside power to rule a huge country.

items.what: Battle of Plassey — Company defeats the Nawab of Bengal
Company gets Diwani (tax rights) of Bengal
Permanent Settlement fixes land revenue in Bengal
Sati banned after Ram Mohan Roy's campaign
Doctrine of Lapse; Awadh annexed 1856
Revolt begins at Meerut; rebels reach Delhi

fig.caption: Key dates behind the picture-story.

check.q: According to the chapter, what helped the British gain power?
options: Indian armies inviting them to rule
check.why: Quarrelling Indian rulers sought British help against rivals, letting the Company gain land and control.

sections.md:
Now the camera moves to the village. The Company needed money to pay its army and its shareholders, so it fixed **heavy land revenue**. Whether rain came or not, the farmer had to pay.

The pictures show a chain of pressure:

- The **Company** demands a fixed sum from the landlord.
- The **landlord (zamindar)** squeezes even more from the peasant.
- The **peasant**, unable to pay, borrows from the **moneylender** at huge interest.
- In a bad year the peasant loses his land and becomes a labourer on it.

One frame shows a family wondering how they will eat after paying the tax. Another shows a moneylender with his account book — the debt only grows. The chapter's point is simple: the new system served the rulers, not those who grew the food.

**Did you know?** In many famines of the period, revenue was still collected. This is why later nationalists called British rule a 'drain of wealth'.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='g' x1='0' x2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#f6d365'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#fda085'/></linearGradient></defs><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fffaf0'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='16' text-anchor='middle'><rect x='20' y='110' width='120' height='70' rx='10' fill='url(#g)'/><text x='80' y='150'>Peasant</text><rect x='170' y='110' width='120' height='70' rx='10' fill='url(#g)'/><text x='230' y='150'>Zamindar</text><rect x='320' y='110' width='120' height='70' rx='10' fill='url(#g)'/><text x='380' y='150'>Company</text><rect x='470' y='110' width='110' height='70' rx='10' fill='#cfd8dc'/><text x='525' y='150'>Britain</text><rect x='120' y='220' width='140' height='50' rx='10' fill='#ef9a9a'/><text x='190' y='250'>Moneylender</text></g><g stroke='#8d4' stroke-width='4' fill='none'><path d='M140 145 H170'/><path d='M290 145 H320'/><path d='M440 145 H470'/></g><circle r='8' fill='#e6a100'><animateMotion dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite' path='M80 110 Q80 90 230 100 T525 110'/></circle><path d='M80 180 Q90 240 120 245' stroke='#c62828' stroke-width='3' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='6 4'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' from='20' to='0' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><text x='300' y='40' font-size='20' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>Where the farmer's rupee went</text></svg>
fig.caption: The coin travels from peasant to zamindar to Company to Britain; debt drags the peasant to the moneylender.
fig.alt: Flow diagram of revenue from peasant to Britain

check.q: Why did peasants fall into the hands of moneylenders?
options: They could not pay the heavy fixed revenue
check.why: Fixed heavy revenue, demanded even in bad years, forced peasants to borrow at high interest.

sections.md:
India's weavers of Dhaka muslin, Bengal silk and Gujarat cotton were once famous across the world. The picture-story shows how British trade policies destroyed them.

- **Cheap machine-made cloth** from factories in Manchester flooded Indian markets almost duty-free.
- **Indian cloth** sent to Britain faced heavy duties, so it could not compete there.
- Weavers were sometimes forced to sell to Company agents at low prices.

One frame shows idle looms and hungry weavers; another shows raw cotton leaving India and finished cloth coming back. India was turned from a maker of goods into a supplier of **raw materials** and a **market** for British products.

This is a key exam idea: *the laws were made to benefit British industry, not Indian people.*
keyTerms: Raw material — unprocessed goods like raw cotton
Duty — a tax on goods crossing a border
Market — the buyers for a product

sections.h: Scene 5: Social evils and Raja Ram Mohan Roy
sections.md:
The chapter is honest that not every problem came from outside. It shows Indian society weighed down by **superstition and harmful customs**: the practice of **sati**, child marriage, the ban on widow remarriage, caste discrimination, and blind faith in rituals and so-called holy men who exploited people.

Into this scene steps **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** (1772–1833) of Bengal. The frames show him arguing that the ancient scriptures did not support sati, writing pamphlets and newspapers, and founding the **Brahmo Samaj (1828)**. He also championed modern education, including English and science. His campaigning helped the government of Lord William Bentinck **ban sati in 1829**.

The chapter also shows that some orthodox people opposed him. Change is never easy — reformers face anger before they win respect.

**Did you know?** Ram Mohan Roy travelled to England in 1830 and died in Bristol in 1833, where a memorial to him still stands.

check.q: Which practice did Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaign against, leading to a ban in 1829?
check.why: His campaign against sati helped persuade the government to ban it in 1829.

sections.md:
As the Company grew stronger, it grew bolder. The picture-story lists grievances:

- **Princes:** states were taken over under the Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur). **Awadh** was annexed in 1856 on the charge of misrule. Pensions of rulers like Nana Saheb were stopped.
- **Religious leaders:** many feared that missionaries and new laws aimed to convert Indians.
- **Sepoys:** Indian soldiers were paid far less than British soldiers, rarely promoted, and from 1856 could be ordered to serve overseas — which some believed would break caste rules.
- **Ordinary people:** heavy taxes, lost jobs at the courts of annexed rulers, and the ruin of crafts.

The frames show discontent building like steam in a closed pot.

The final scenes show the explosion. The new **Enfield rifle** used cartridges which, it was rumoured, were greased with **cow and pig fat** — offensive to both Hindus and Muslims, since the cartridge had to be bitten open.

- At **Barrackpore** in March 1857, sepoy **Mangal Pandey** attacked his officers and was hanged.
- On **10 May 1857** sepoys at **Meerut** rebelled, freed their jailed comrades and marched to **Delhi**.
- They proclaimed the old Mughal emperor **Bahadur Shah Zafar** their leader.
- The revolt spread to Kanpur (Nana Saheb), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh) and elsewhere.

The picture-story ends here, with India rising. Historically the British crushed the revolt by 1858, and the Crown took over India from the Company. But the chapter's message is that 1857 was the first great united challenge to British rule.

check.q: Where did the sepoys first revolt on 10 May 1857?
check.why: The Meerut sepoys rebelled on 10 May 1857 and marched to Delhi.

sections.md:
**How to read the chapter:** look at the drawing first, then the caption, then the speech bubble. Ask: *Who is speaking? What do they want? What does the artist want me to feel?*

**Themes:** disunity and its cost; economic exploitation; social reform from within; the build-up of anger into rebellion.

**Language work in this chapter:** the exercises ask you to list the reasons for discontent, to match people to events, and to write a short account from the point of view of a character (a weaver, a sepoy, a farmer). Practise using **past tense** narration and linking words: *because, so, as a result, therefore*.

**Model answer — Why did the sepoys revolt?** The sepoys were paid less than British soldiers and denied promotion. The rule to serve overseas hurt their religious beliefs. Finally the rumour that the new cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat made them feel their faith was being attacked. Their anger, joined with the grievances of princes and peasants, broke out at Meerut in May 1857.

summary: The chapter is a picture-story of about 1757–1857.
Weak Mughal power and quarrelling rulers let the East India Company grow.
Plassey (1757) and the Diwani (1765) gave the Company a base in Bengal.
Heavy land revenue ruined peasants and enriched moneylenders.
British trade laws destroyed Indian weaving; India became a raw-material supplier.
Social evils like sati and child marriage weakened society.
Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj and helped ban sati (1829).
The Doctrine of Lapse and annexation of Awadh angered princes.
Sepoys faced low pay, no promotion and religious fears.
The greased-cartridge rumour sparked the 1857 revolt at Meerut.
Rebels made Bahadur Shah Zafar their emperor in Delhi.
practice: What was the condition of India before the British took control?
How did the Company take advantage of quarrels between Indian rulers?
Describe the problems faced by Indian farmers under Company rule.
How did British laws ruin Indian weavers?
Write a note on the work of Raja Ram Mohan Roy.
List four reasons for the discontent of the sepoys.
What was the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857?
Imagine you are a weaver in 1820. Write a diary entry about your life.
Why is the picture-story form useful for telling history?

rd-school-c8-english.ch03-glimpses-of-th.title: Glimpses of the Past — Chapter Companion (part 2)
rd-school-c8-english.ch03-glimpses-of-th.subtitle: A timeline from 1757 to 1857, key people, and exam practice

sections.md:
The chapter moves quickly through about a hundred years, from the Company's rise to the revolt of 1857. Fixing the order of events makes it far easier to answer questions.

Alongside the picture-story, remember that history textbooks describe the British East India Company first coming as **traders**, then taking advantage of quarrels among Indian rulers, and slowly becoming a **ruling power** with its own army of Indian soldiers (sepoys). Its policies hurt farmers, weavers, soldiers and rulers alike, and the anger finally burst out in 1857.

items.what: Battle of Plassey: the Company gains power in Bengal
Permanent Settlement of land revenue in Bengal
Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigns against social evils and for modern education
Sati banned by law
English education promoted officially
Annexation of Awadh
Revolt begins at Meerut (10 May); sepoys march to Delhi

fig.caption: Key dates behind the picture-story. Verify any date asked in your exam with your history textbook.

check.q: Where did the revolt of 1857 begin?
check.why: Sepoys at Meerut rose on 10 May 1857 and marched to Delhi, starting the revolt.

sections.h: Who is who, and why it matters
sections.md:
- **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** — a social reformer from Bengal who argued against sati, child marriage and the ill-treatment of women, and supported modern education. He also started newspapers and wrote in favour of a free press. In the chapter he speaks for reform and reason.
- **The Company officials** — shown as greedy and uncaring, interested in profit and power.
- **Moneylenders and landlords** — who squeezed poor farmers with high interest and rent.
- **The weavers and craftsmen** — ruined when cheap machine-made cloth from Britain flooded Indian markets.
- **The sepoys** — Indian soldiers in the Company army, angered by low pay, being sent overseas, and the rumour that new cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat.
- **Bahadur Shah Zafar** — the last Mughal emperor, whom the rebels declared their leader in Delhi.

**Why it matters:** the chapter shows that 1857 was not caused by one thing. Economic ruin, social interference and insults to soldiers all added up.

check.q: What rumour angered the sepoys in 1857?
options: New cartridges were greased with animal fat
check.why: The rumour that cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat offended both Hindu and Muslim soldiers.

sections.h: Exercise topics: working with the text and language
sections.md:
**Working with the text** asks you to:
- Describe the condition of Indian rulers when the Company arrived, and how the Company used their quarrels.
- Explain how farmers were trapped by landlords and moneylenders.
- Describe the effect of British laws and taxes on weavers and traders.
- Say what Raja Ram Mohan Roy wanted to change and why.
- List the reasons for the soldiers' anger.

**Reading pictures:** the chapter is a comic strip. When answering, combine what the picture shows (faces, clothes, setting) with the speech bubbles. A good answer says *who* is speaking, *what* is happening and *what feeling* the picture conveys.

**Writing tasks:** turn one frame into a short paragraph of narrative; or write a dialogue between a weaver and a moneylender; or imagine you are a sepoy in 1857 writing a letter home. Keep historical facts correct and do not invent dates.

**Language:** practise words such as *tyranny, revolt, reform, exploitation, annexation* — use each in a sentence of your own.

**Official text:** read the full picture-story free in *Honeydew* (Class 8) on ncert.nic.in.
keyTerms: Sepoy — Indian soldier in the Company army
Annexation — taking over a state's territory
Reform — change to improve society
Revolt — open uprising against authority

summary: The Company came as traders and became rulers.
Plassey (1757) gave it power in Bengal.
Farmers suffered from landlords, moneylenders and high revenue.
Weavers were ruined by cheap British machine-made cloth.
Raja Ram Mohan Roy fought sati and promoted education.
Sati was banned in 1829.
Sepoys were angered by low pay, overseas service and greased cartridges.
The revolt began at Meerut in May 1857; Bahadur Shah Zafar was declared leader.
Reading a comic: combine picture and speech bubble.
practice: How did the Company take advantage of Indian rulers?
Describe the condition of Indian farmers in the period shown.
Why did Indian weavers lose their livelihood?
What reforms did Raja Ram Mohan Roy want?
Give three reasons for the revolt of 1857.
Write a letter from a sepoy in 1857 to his family.
Write a dialogue between a farmer and a moneylender.

rd-school-c8-english.ch04-bepin-choudhur.title: Bepin Choudhury's Lapse of Memory — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch04-bepin-choudhur.subtitle: A man who never forgets is told he went to Ranchi. He has no memory of it. Is he going mad?

sections.h: The hook: a stranger who remembers you
sections.md:
Have you ever had someone greet you warmly, recall a trip you took together — and you have no idea who they are? Now imagine you are a man who prides himself on a perfect memory. That is the nightmare at the heart of this story by **Satyajit Ray** (1921–1992), the great Bengali film-maker and writer, translated into English by Gopa Majumdar.

Because Ray's work is still under copyright, this companion does **not** reproduce the story. Instead it retells every scene in our own words, explains what each part means, and prepares you for exams. Read the original in your Honeydew textbook (link at the end).

**Who's who**

| Character | Role |
|---|---|
| Bepin Choudhury | Office worker in Calcutta; proud, solitary, loves crime and ghost stories |
| Parimal Ghosh | A stranger who claims they met in Ranchi |
| Seth (Dinesh Mukerji) | Bepin's old friend; is he in on something? |
| Chunilal | Old school friend; down on his luck; asked Bepin for a job |
| Dr. Chanda (Paresh Chanda) | Nerve specialist Bepin consults |
| Bepin's servant | Minor; sees him come and go |

Every Monday on his way home from office, Bepin Choudhury stops at **Kalicharan's bookshop in New Market**, Calcutta, to buy crime stories, ghost stories and thrillers. He needs at least five a week, because he reads them all.

This Monday, as he is about to leave, a stout, round-faced man greets him by name. The stranger, **Parimal Ghosh**, says they met in **Ranchi in 1958**, during the Puja holidays: Bepin had gone there, they had travelled together in a car, and even visited the **Hudroo Falls**. Bepin is puzzled — he has never been to Ranchi in his life. He politely says the man must be mistaken.

Parimal Ghosh insists, and then adds two stunning details: Bepin had **sprained his ankle** at the falls, and he had stayed at a bungalow with a man named **Dinesh Mukerji**. Bepin, annoyed, leaves.

**What the scene shows:** Bepin is a creature of habit, confident and a little arrogant about his memory. The stranger's precise details plant a seed of doubt.

check.q: Where did Parimal Ghosh claim to have met Bepin Babu?
check.why: He said they met in Ranchi in 1958 during the Puja holidays.

sections.md:
At home, Bepin tries to dismiss the meeting. He reads a new crime novel, but cannot concentrate. Facts swim in his head: Hudroo Falls, the sprain, Dinesh Mukerji. He asks himself honestly: has his memory ever failed? No — he remembers everything; he has a remarkable memory.

But it is a fact that he did go somewhere in the Puja of 1958 — or did he? He cannot recall clearly. The fear grows: if he went to Ranchi and forgot it completely, then something is badly wrong with his mind.

**Ray's craft:** notice how the author shows the mind working — questions, half-answers, and the slow growth of anxiety. This is *suspense*: we, like Bepin, don't know the truth yet.
keyTerms: Lapse — a temporary failure
Suspense — tension about what will happen next

sections.md:
Bepin decides to settle the matter. Dinesh Mukerji is an old acquaintance, so Bepin phones him and asks, cautiously, whether he went to Ranchi in 1958.

Dinesh says: *of course* — Bepin was there, and so was Dinesh. He adds that Bepin had indeed **hurt his foot** at the falls. Worse, Dinesh hints that Bepin seems to be unwell if he cannot remember.

Now Bepin is shaken. Two people agree on the same story. He goes back over his own memory — the sprain, a limp, a doctor's visit — and finds nothing. Could he be losing his mind?

check.q: What did Dinesh Mukerji say when Bepin phoned him?
options: Bepin had gone to Ranchi and hurt his foot
He had gone to Ranchi alone
check.why: Dinesh backed up Parimal's account, which deepened Bepin's fear.

sections.md:
Desperate, Bepin visits **Dr. Paresh Chanda**, a young nerve specialist. After hearing the story the doctor says this is an unusual case; he has read of memory loss after a head injury or shock, but Bepin has had neither.

The doctor offers pills, but admits there is no sure cure. His other suggestion is to **go to Ranchi** — seeing the places might bring the memory back.

Bepin goes. He sees Hudroo Falls and walks around. Nothing returns: the place feels completely new. On the way back he is so upset that he collapses. A man helps him home.

This is the **climax** of Bepin's fear: the trip meant to cure him seems to prove that his mind is gone.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#eef6ff'/><polyline points='30,260 120,230 210,190 300,140 390,80 470,60 560,230' fill='none' stroke='#d84315' stroke-width='5' stroke-dasharray='900' stroke-dashoffset='900'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' from='900' to='0' dur='4s' fill='freeze'/></polyline><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle'><text x='30' y='285'>Bookshop</text><text x='120' y='255'>Doubt</text><text x='210' y='215'>Phone call</text><text x='300' y='165'>Doctor</text><text x='390' y='105'>Ranchi</text><text x='470' y='45'>Collapse</text><text x='545' y='255'>Truth</text></g><text x='300' y='30' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'>Bepin's rising fear</text></svg>
fig.caption: The plot as a graph of Bepin's anxiety: it climbs until the twist brings it crashing down.
fig.alt: Line graph of anxiety rising then falling

sections.md:
Back home, Bepin's servant hands him a letter delivered by hand. It is from **Chunilal**, an old school friend who had recently come to Bepin asking for a job. Bepin, busy and impatient, had refused him rudely.

In the letter Chunilal confesses: he arranged the whole thing. Bepin had once boasted that he could never be fooled; and Chunilal, hurt by his refusal, decided to teach him a lesson. Parimal Ghosh and Dinesh Mukerji joined in. Bepin **never went to Ranchi**. Chunilal adds that Dr. Chanda might also be in on it — and that the pills are only sugar. Bepin's memory is perfectly fine.

In some versions Chunilal also says he hopes Bepin will remember to be kinder to friends in need.

**The meaning:** the 'lapse of memory' was not in Bepin's brain but in his heart — he had forgotten old friendship and the duty to help.

check.q: Why did Chunilal play the trick?
options: To teach Bepin a lesson for being unkind
check.why: Bepin had rudely refused to help Chunilal when he was in trouble, so Chunilal decided to teach him a lesson.

sections.md:
**Themes**
- *Pride and humility:* Bepin is proud of his memory and his self-sufficiency; the trick humbles him.
- *Friendship and responsibility:* old ties carry duties; ignoring them has consequences.
- *Power of suggestion:* if enough people tell you something, you may begin to doubt your own mind.

**Bepin Choudhury:** a loner, disciplined, a lover of thrillers, sure of himself, rather self-centred. By the end we feel sympathy for him, and also see why he deserved the lesson.

**Chunilal:** clever, wounded, mischievous; his trick is cruel but not malicious — it ends with truth and a moral.

**Ray's craft:** a calm, realistic opening; small concrete details (New Market, Hudroo Falls, the sprain) that make the lie believable; suspense built scene by scene; and a final **twist** that makes us re-read everything. Irony: a man who devours detective stories becomes the victim of a mystery he cannot solve.

**Language work:** the exercises ask you to find words for feelings (*irritated, worried, desperate*), to use *must have / might have* to guess what happened, and to change direct speech into reported speech.

workedExamples.q: Change into reported speech: Parimal said, "You sprained your ankle at Hudroo Falls."
steps: Reporting verb is past (said), so shift tense back.
workedExamples.answer: Parimal said that Bepin had sprained his ankle at Hudroo Falls.

workedExamples.q: Use 'must have': Bepin remembered nothing of Ranchi.
steps: 'Must have' shows a strong guess about the past.
workedExamples.answer: Bepin must not have gone to Ranchi at all.

rd-school-c8-english.ch04-bepin-choudhur.title: Bepin Choudhury's Lapse of Memory — Chapter Companion (part 2)
rd-school-c8-english.ch04-bepin-choudhur.subtitle: The author, the clues, the motive — and how to answer like a detective

sections.md: The story was written by **Satyajit Ray** (1921–1992), one of India's greatest film-makers and a much-loved Bengali writer. He directed *Pather Panchali* and received an honorary Oscar in 1992, as well as the Bharat Ratna. For young readers he created the detective **Feluda** and the scientist **Professor Shonku**. His stories are known for crisp plots, everyday Kolkata settings, gentle humour and a twist at the end — all of which you see in this story, which was originally written in Bengali and is read in English translation in your textbook.

check.q: Satyajit Ray is best known as a…
check.why: Ray was a celebrated film-maker who also wrote popular stories for young readers.

sections.h: Rereading as a detective: the clues
sections.md:
A good twist is fair: the clues are there from the start. On a second reading, notice these:

1. **The stranger knows too much.** Parimal Ghose describes the trip to Ranchi in great detail — the place, the waterfall (Hudru Falls), the car, even an accident Bepin supposedly had. Such detail is meant to convince Bepin, and us.
2. **Bepin's memory is otherwise excellent.** He is a methodical man who remembers small things. A whole trip vanishing from his memory is strange.
3. **His friends all seem to agree.** Dinesh Mukerji, whom he phones, also says Bepin went to Ranchi. This makes Bepin panic — but it also hints at a plan involving several people.
4. **Chunilal.** He is mentioned as an old school friend who had fallen on hard times and had asked Bepin for help, which Bepin refused. A good reader remembers him.
5. **The doctor's calm.** Dr Chatterjee says this is not a case for medicines and suggests Bepin visit Ranchi himself — the visit only makes things worse.

The ending reveals that **Chunilal** arranged the whole trick. Bepin had not gone to Ranchi at all; Chunilal had persuaded others to play along. In his letter he explains that this was his way of making Bepin suffer a little, because Bepin had refused to help him when he was in need. He also hints that a small sum of money could help 'cure' the problem.

check.q: Why did Chunilal play the trick on Bepin?
options: Because Bepin had refused to help him in his time of need
check.why: Chunilal's letter shows he wanted to teach Bepin a lesson for turning him away when he needed help.

sections.md:
- **Selfishness and its cost** — Bepin is comfortable, orderly and self-absorbed. He ignored a friend's distress; the trick makes him feel helpless in turn.
- **Fear of losing one's mind** — the story shows how quickly a confident person can be shaken when he cannot trust his own memory.
- **Irony** — the man who prides himself on his perfect memory is the one 'diagnosed' with a lapse; and the doctor's 'cure' (a visit to Ranchi) is pointless because there was never a trip.
- **Moral** — kindness to friends matters; but readers can also discuss whether Chunilal's revenge was fair or cruel. A balanced answer sees both sides.

**Exercise topics:** comprehension questions on why Bepin went to New Market; why he could not recall the Ranchi trip; what the doctor advised; what the letter revealed. **Language work** includes word meanings in context, idioms, and turning the story into a play: a list of characters, short stage directions and dialogue for the scene at the bookshop or the doctor's clinic.

**Official text:** read the full story free in *Honeydew* (Class 8) on ncert.nic.in.
keyTerms: Lapse of memory — a failure to remember
Twist — an unexpected turn at the end
Irony — outcome opposite to what is expected
Motive — reason for an action

rd-school-c8-english.ch05-summit-within.title: The Summit Within — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch05-summit-within.subtitle: He stood on top of Everest — and found that the hardest mountain was inside him

sections.h: The hook: what do you feel on top of the world?
sections.md:
In **May 1965**, members of an Indian expedition stood on the summit of **Mount Everest** (8,848 m), the highest point on Earth. One of them was **Major H.P.S. Ahluwalia**, an army officer. Later he wrote a short, thoughtful essay about that moment. It is not a story of ropes and ice axes; it is about *feelings* — and about the 'mountain' every person must climb inside.

This companion retells and explains the essay paragraph by paragraph in our own words (the original is in your Honeydew textbook — link below).

**Did you know?** The 1965 Indian expedition, led by Commander **M.S. Kohli**, put **nine climbers** on the summit — a record that stood for many years. Ahluwalia was later badly injured in the 1965 war and spent his life working for people with disabilities, which gives his essay extra meaning.

fig.alt: Animated climber reaching a peak

sections.h: Paragraph 1: Mixed feelings at the top
sections.md:
The writer says people often ask him what he felt on top of Everest. His answer: a mixture of emotions that are hard to put in words.

- **Joy and achievement** — the goal of years was reached.
- **Humility** — he felt small before the vastness of nature, and grateful.
- **Sadness** — a strange feeling that there was nothing higher to climb; all roads now lead down.

He compares this to life: success brings joy but also a sense of 'what next?'

**Meaning:** great achievements are not just thrilling; they are deep, quiet and humbling.

check.q: Which feeling did the writer NOT describe at the summit?
options: Sadness that there was nowhere higher
check.why: He felt joy, humility and a touch of sadness — never a wish to beat others.

sections.md:
The essay asks the famous question: *why do people climb mountains?* The quick reply, 'because it is there', is not enough for Ahluwalia.

- Mountains are **nature at its best**: beautiful, grand, challenging.
- Climbing tests **endurance, persistence and will-power**.
- Overcoming danger and hardship gives a lasting **sense of achievement**.

He says the climber comes closer to nature and, in a way, closer to God. On the summit he felt deep awe — a spiritual experience.
keyTerms: Endurance — the ability to keep going through hardship
Persistence — not giving up
Exhilaration — great excitement and joy

sections.md:
Ahluwalia describes the sacred things climbers left on top:

| Climber | Offering |
|---|---|
| Rawat | a picture of Goddess Durga |
| Phu Dorji | a relic of the Buddha |
| Ahluwalia | a picture of Guru Nanak |
| Edmund Hillary (1953) | had buried a cross in the snow |

**Meaning:** at the top of the world, people of different faiths gave thanks side by side. Nature unites us; the summit is a place of humility, not conquest. The writer felt they were not 'conquering' the mountain but being allowed to stand on it.

check.q: What did Phu Dorji leave on the summit?
check.why: Phu Dorji left a relic of the Buddha, showing the shared spirit of many faiths.

sections.md:
From the top, the writer saw great peaks — Lhotse, Nuptse, Makalu — lying below, and clouds far beneath. Mountains that look enormous from the valley seemed small. He felt a strange loneliness too.

Then came the realisation that the climb down is as dangerous as the climb up. Many accidents happen on the descent, when the body is tired and the mind relaxes. The summit is not the end.

**Meaning:** after success, stay humble and careful.

Here is the heart of the essay. Climbing Everest is a **physical** climb, but there is another climb that is **emotional** and **spiritual**: overcoming fear, anger, jealousy, laziness and selfishness in ourselves.

That inner mountain is just as high and as hard. It needs the same qualities: endurance, persistence, will-power. Ahluwalia says the climb of the 'summit within' is as satisfying as — even more than — the physical one.

**Meaning:** every person faces an inner Everest. When you control a bad temper, keep studying after failing, or forgive a friend, you are climbing your summit within.

check.q: What is 'the summit within'?
check.why: It is the inner climb — conquering fear, anger and other weaknesses inside ourselves.

sections.md:
The essay ends with the writer saying that the climb changed him: he became more humble, more aware of nature's power and of his own smallness, and more determined to keep climbing the inner peaks.

**Tone:** reflective, sincere, spiritual, humble. **Style:** first person; short narrative moments mixed with reflections; rhetorical questions; images of height and depth.

**Themes:** courage and endurance; humility before nature; unity of faiths; the inner struggle; growth through challenge.

**Vocabulary** (meanings in our words): *exhilarating* — thrillingly happy; *ecstasy* — overwhelming joy; *humble* — modest; *awe* — wonder mixed with respect; *ascent / descent* — going up / coming down; *summit* — top.

**Grammar focus:** the exercises practise forming words and opposites (e.g. *ascent/descent*, *possible/impossible*), and ask you to write about a challenge you faced.

**Model answer — What qualities does a mountaineer need?** A mountaineer needs fitness and endurance to bear cold, thin air and exhaustion; persistence and will-power to go on after setbacks; teamwork and trust; and humility, because the mountain is never truly 'conquered'. The same qualities help us climb the inner summit.

**Did you know?** At 8,848 m the air holds only about one-third of the oxygen available at sea level, so most climbers use bottled oxygen.

rd-school-c8-english.ch05-summit-within-.title: The Summit Within — Chapter Companion (part 2)
rd-school-c8-english.ch05-summit-within-.subtitle: The 1965 expedition, the climb itself, the author's ideas, and exam practice

sections.h: About the author and the 1965 expedition
sections.md:
The chapter is a personal essay by **Major H.P.S. Ahluwalia**, an Indian Army officer who was a member of the **Indian expedition that climbed Mount Everest in 1965**. That expedition, led by **Captain M.S. Kohli**, was the first fully Indian team to succeed, and it placed nine climbers on the summit in a series of summit attempts in May 1965 — a world record at the time. Ahluwalia reached the top along with his companions in one of these parties. After the expedition he was honoured with awards including the Arjuna Award and the Padma Shri. Later in the 1965 war he was seriously injured and used a wheelchair, but he went on to work for people with disabilities — a living example of the 'summit within' he writes about.

Mount Everest (Sagarmatha in Nepali, Chomolungma in Tibetan) is the highest peak on earth at about **8,849 m** above sea level (the height agreed by Nepal and China in 2020). It was first climbed in 1953 by Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary.

check.q: Who led the 1965 Indian Everest expedition?
check.why: Captain M.S. Kohli led the 1965 expedition, in which Ahluwalia was one of the summiters.

sections.h: Why climbing Everest is so hard
sections.md:
To understand the author's feelings, picture the climb itself:

- **Thin air** — near the top, the air has only about one-third of the oxygen available at sea level. Climbers carry oxygen cylinders; every step is slow and tiring.
- **Cold and wind** — temperatures can drop far below –30 °C, and fierce winds can cause frostbite in minutes.
- **Danger** — crevasses (deep cracks in the glacier), avalanches, the icefall near base camp, and sudden storms.
- **The mind** — fatigue, fear and loneliness test a climber's will as much as the body.

The author's point is that the physical summit demands great **endurance, persistence and willpower**, and that these same qualities help us climb the 'mountains' of ordinary life.

check.q: Why do climbers near Everest's summit use oxygen cylinders?
options: Because the air has much less oxygen there
check.why: At very high altitude the air holds far less oxygen, so extra oxygen helps the body keep working.

sections.h: The central idea in plain words
sections.md:
The essay moves from the outer climb to an inner one. Its argument, in our own words:

1. Standing on the top, the author feels **joy and pride**, but also **humility** and a touch of **sadness** — sad that there is no higher place to climb, and aware of how small he is before nature.
2. People climb mountains because of the challenge, the wish to push one's limits, and the beauty and sense of nearness to the divine that high places give.
3. The climbers leave offerings on the summit as a mark of reverence — each according to his faith.
4. Looking down, he sees the surrounding peaks spread below and feels both triumph and a desire to go beyond.
5. The **'summit within'** is the struggle with one's own weaknesses — fear, laziness, anger, doubt. This inner summit is harder and more rewarding to reach than any peak.
6. The experience changes a person for ever: after one has climbed, one is always drawn back to the mountains, and the lessons stay for life.

The essay's message: **every person has a mountain inside to conquer**, and the same qualities — endurance, persistence and will — help in both climbs.

check.q: What does the 'summit within' refer to?
options: A hidden peak in the Himalayas
Overcoming one's own inner weaknesses and limits
check.why: The author uses the summit as a metaphor for conquering our inner fears and failings.

rd-school-c8-english.ch06-jodys-fawn.title: This is Jody's Fawn — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch06-jodys-fawn.subtitle: A boy, a dying doe, and a baby deer alone in the Florida woods

sections.h: The hook: a life for a life
sections.md:
A rattlesnake bites a father in the woods. To save him, he shoots a **doe** (a female deer), cuts out her heart and liver and presses them on the bite to draw out the poison. He lives. But somewhere in the bushes, the doe's newborn **fawn** is now alone. A boy can't stop thinking about it.

This chapter is taken from the American novel ***The Yearling*** (1938) by **Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings** (1896–1953), which won the Pulitzer Prize. It is set in the scrub forest of **Florida** among poor farming families. The author died in 1953, but because we are not certain of the exact wording of the textbook extract, this companion gives a **complete scene-by-scene retelling in our own words** with the meaning of every part. Read the original in your Honeydew book (link below).

**Characters**

| Who | Role |
|---|---|
| Jody Baxter | 11–12-year-old boy, kind and imaginative |
| Penny Baxter | his father, bitten by a rattlesnake |
| Ma Baxter | his mother, practical and firm |
| Doc Wilson | the doctor who treated Penny |
| Mill-wheel | son of the Forrester family, a neighbour |

Penny Baxter is recovering in bed after the snakebite. Doc Wilson has done his work. Jody cannot rest: he keeps thinking of the doe whose organs saved his father, and of her fawn, now motherless and probably starving.

He goes to his father and asks, gently, whether he may go and find the fawn and bring it home. Penny agrees at once: it is not right, he says, to repay the doe by leaving her baby to die. He says they took the mother; they owe the fawn its life. Ma Baxter is less happy — they barely have enough milk and food themselves — but Penny's word wins. Doc Wilson also says the boy is right.

**Meaning:** gratitude and responsibility. Penny teaches Jody that we owe something to those who help us, even animals.

check.q: Why does Penny agree that Jody should bring the fawn home?
options: Because they owed the doe for saving his life
check.why: Penny felt it would be ungrateful to let the fawn starve after its mother's death saved him.

sections.md:
Jody needs help to find the place. **Mill-wheel**, a Forrester boy, is riding back home and takes Jody along on his horse. On the way Jody worries that Mill-wheel might laugh at him or that the fawn might already be dead — eaten by wildcats or other animals.

Mill-wheel is a bit doubtful; he warns that the fawn may have been taken by an animal, and that a fawn raised by people grows up tame and later causes trouble. But he takes Jody to the spot where Penny shot the doe and says he will leave Jody there because Jody wants to look alone.

**Meaning:** Jody's determination. He wants to do the job himself, quietly.
keyTerms: Doe — female deer
Fawn — a baby deer
Yearling — an animal about one year old

sections.md:
Jody finds the body of the doe where it fell, with buzzards circling. He searches the area, following small hoof prints, and at last discovers the **fawn** curled up in a hidden nest of grass. It lifts its head and looks at him with big, wet eyes.

Jody is overwhelmed with tenderness. He strokes it; it doesn't run away. He feels its soft, spotted coat. He picks it up — its legs dangle — and carries it, staggering under its weight, through the woods. When he sets it down to rest, it follows him on wobbly legs, as if it knows him already.

**Meaning:** a deep bond forms instantly. The scene is full of sensory detail: smell of the woods, softness of the fawn, Jody's beating heart.

fig.caption: After a rest, the fawn trots behind Jody as if he were its mother.
fig.alt: Animated boy walking with a fawn following

sections.h: Scene 4: Home and a bottle of milk
sections.md:
Jody reaches home. Ma Baxter is not pleased, but she has agreed. The fawn will not drink milk from a bowl. Jody dips his fingers in the milk and lets it suck them; slowly it learns to drink from the gourd. Every time he moves, it follows him.

Penny watches with a smile. Jody feels that the fawn is truly his — the first thing that has ever belonged to him alone. He thinks of naming it (in the novel it becomes **Flag**, after its white tail).

**Meaning:** patience and care. Jody becomes a 'parent' and learns responsibility.

check.q: How did Jody get the fawn to drink milk?
options: He let it suck milk from his fingers
check.why: The fawn would not drink from a bowl, so Jody dipped his fingers in milk and let it suck them.

sections.md:
**Themes**
- *Compassion for animals* — Jody cannot bear the fawn to suffer.
- *Gratitude and debt* — the doe gave her life; the family repays by saving her baby.
- *Growing up* — Jody takes on adult responsibility.
- *Bond between humans and nature* — life in the scrub is hard, yet full of tenderness.

**Jody:** sensitive, kind, imaginative, determined, responsible. **Penny:** fair, wise, grateful; a gentle father. **Ma Baxter:** practical and worried about food, but not cruel. **Mill-wheel:** sceptical but helpful. **Doc Wilson:** supports Jody's idea.

**Style:** third-person narration close to Jody's feelings; American rural dialogue; rich nature imagery.

**Did you know?** In the full novel, the fawn grows into a yearling that eats the family's crops, leading to a heartbreaking ending — Jody's painful step into adulthood.

The exercises focus on:

- **Comprehension** of why Jody went, what Mill-wheel thought, and how the fawn responded.
- **Vocabulary of movement and sounds** — *stagger, wobble, bleat, trot*.
- **Adverbs** describing how things are done (*gently, slowly, firmly*).
- **Writing:** a paragraph on caring for a pet, or a debate on keeping wild animals at home.

**Model answer — Why did Jody want to bring the fawn home?** Jody knew his father's life had been saved by the doe's heart and liver. The doe's baby was now alone and would starve or be killed. Feeling grateful and sorry for it, he wanted to repay the mother by caring for the fawn.

**Model answer — How did the fawn respond to Jody?** At first it simply looked at him without fear. When he carried and then put it down, it followed him, and later it learnt to drink milk from his fingers. It treated him like a mother.

rd-school-c8-english.ch06-jodys-fawn-2.title: This is Jody's Fawn — Chapter Companion (part 2)
rd-school-c8-english.ch06-jodys-fawn-2.subtitle: Deeper reading, the comprehension checks, language work and exam answers

sections.h: Reading closely: Jody's mind, step by step
sections.md:
The extract is short, but almost every paragraph shows a change inside Jody. Follow it like a graph of feelings.

1. **Guilt and pity.** As the family rests after the crisis, Jody keeps returning to one thought: the doe died so that his father could live, and her baby is out there alone. He feels the fawn is, in a way, *his* responsibility.
2. **Courage to ask.** Ma Baxter has already complained that there is little food to spare. Jody still asks his father directly — a brave step for a boy in a poor household.
3. **Support from adults.** Penny says it would be ungrateful to let the fawn starve; Doc Wilson agrees that the boy is right. Jody feels respected — his idea is treated as an adult idea.
4. **Fear on the road.** Riding behind Mill-wheel, Jody imagines the worst: that a wildcat or buzzards have reached the fawn first. Note how the author lets us share his anxious thoughts.
5. **Wanting privacy.** At the spot, Jody asks to search alone. If the fawn is dead, he does not want anyone to see his grief; if it is alive, he wants the first meeting to be his.
6. **Joy and tenderness.** When he finds it alive, his fear changes to love. He moves slowly so as not to frighten it.
7. **Pride and belonging.** By the end the fawn trusts him, and Jody feels it truly belongs to him.

**Exam tip:** questions such as *'How did Jody's feelings change?'* reward answers that follow this order with one example for each step.

check.q: Why did Jody want to look for the fawn alone?
options: He did not want anyone to see him if the fawn was dead, and wanted the first meeting to be private
check.why: Jody wanted privacy both for his possible grief and for the special moment of finding the fawn alive.

sections.h: Mill-wheel's warning and the adults' views
sections.md:
The story gives us **three adult attitudes**, and exam questions often ask you to compare them.

| Person | Attitude | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Penny | Strongly in favour | Gratitude; it is fair to repay the doe |
| Doc Wilson | In favour | Thinks nothing in this world is free; the debt must be paid |
| Ma Baxter | Reluctant | Worried about milk and food for the family |
| Mill-wheel | Doubtful but helpful | Fears the fawn may be dead; thinks a pet deer is a nuisance |

Notice that nobody in the story is a villain. Ma Baxter's worry is realistic: on a poor farm, a growing animal is another mouth to feed. Mill-wheel's doubts are also sensible. Rawlings shows that kindness sometimes has a cost — and that good people may disagree.

**Did you know?** The phrase 'a yearling' in the novel's title refers both to the deer, which grows to a year old, and quietly to Jody himself, who is growing up during that year.
keyTerms: Sceptical — doubtful, not easily convinced
Reluctant — unwilling, but going along
Debt of gratitude — the duty to repay kindness

sections.h: How Jody handles the fawn: patience as a skill
sections.md:
Look at the practical things Jody does. They show that caring needs both love and skill.

- He **approaches slowly** and speaks softly so the fawn does not bolt.
- He **strokes** it before trying to lift it, letting it get used to his smell and touch.
- He **carries** it in his arms, its legs hanging, though it is heavy and he must stop to rest.
- When he puts it down, he **walks on** and lets it decide to follow him — trust is earned, not forced.
- At home, when it will not drink from the gourd, he **dips his fingers** in milk and lets it suck, then lowers his fingers into the milk so it learns to drink.

This is how real fawns and calves are hand-reared: young mammals instinctively suck, so a finger works better than a bowl at first.

**Discussion:** Is it a good idea to take a wild animal home? In India, keeping deer or other wild animals is illegal under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. If you find an orphaned wild animal, the right step is to inform the forest department or a wildlife rescue centre.

check.q: What does Jody's way of feeding the fawn show?
options: Patience and understanding of the animal
That he was in a hurry
check.why: Instead of forcing it, Jody patiently used his milk-dipped fingers until the fawn learnt to drink.

sections.h: Working with the text: model answers
sections.md:
**1. Why did Penny Baxter allow Jody to bring the fawn home?**
Penny had killed the doe to use her heart and liver to draw out the snake's poison. He felt it would be ungrateful to let her fawn starve, so he agreed that Jody should bring it home and raise it.

**2. What did Doc Wilson mean by 'Nothing in the world ever comes quite free'?** (meaning in our words)
He meant that everything has a price: Penny's life was bought with the doe's life, so the family owed something in return — the care of the fawn.

**3. How did Jody find the fawn?**
He went to the place where the doe lay, searched the bushes, and noticed a small movement in a clump of grass. There the fawn lay hidden. It looked at him without fear.

**4. How did Jody bring the fawn back?**
He lifted it into his arms and carried it, resting when he was tired. Then he set it down and it followed him the rest of the way.

**5. Why was Ma Baxter unhappy?**
She worried that there was barely enough milk and food for the family. A fawn would need feeding for months.

**6. How did Jody teach the fawn to drink?**
By letting it suck milk off his fingers and gradually lowering his hand into the gourd of milk.

**A. Adverbs of manner.** Many exercises ask you to describe *how* someone did something.
- Jody walked *quietly*. The fawn moved *unsteadily*. Penny spoke *firmly*. Ma Baxter agreed *reluctantly*.
To form many adverbs, add **-ly** to an adjective: *gentle → gently, slow → slowly, happy → happily, careful → carefully.*

**B. Reported (indirect) speech.** The story has lots of dialogue. Practise:
- Direct: Penny said, "You can bring the fawn home."
- Indirect: Penny said that Jody could bring the fawn home.
- Direct: Jody asked, "May I go to look for it?"
- Indirect: Jody asked if he might go to look for it.
Rules: change the tense one step back (*can → could, is → was*), change pronouns, and remove quotation marks.

**C. Phrases from the story** (meanings): *to be in the way* — to cause trouble; *to make up one's mind* — to decide; *a lump in the throat* — a strong emotion that makes it hard to speak.

**D. Speaking and writing.** Imagine you are Jody. Write a diary entry for the night the fawn came home: how you felt, what worried you, what you will name it. (About 120 words: date, feelings, events, closing thought.)

check.q: Change to indirect speech: Ma said, "We have no milk to spare."
options: Ma said that we have no milk to spare.
Ma said that they had no milk to spare.
Ma said they have had no milk.
Ma says they had no milk.
check.why: The pronoun 'we' becomes 'they' and the present 'have' moves back to the past 'had'.
