rd-school-c8-science-a.ch02-microorganis.title: Microorganisms: Friend and Foe
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch02-microorganis.subtitle: The invisible crowd that makes your curd, bakes your bread — and sometimes makes you sick

sections.md:
Leave a slice of bread in a damp box for a few days. Grey-green fuzz appears. Put a spoon of old curd into warm milk at night, and by morning the whole bowl has set. Who did that? Not you. A crowd of living things too small for your eyes did the work.

Living organisms so small that they cannot be seen with the naked eye are called **microorganisms** or **microbes**. Some can be seen with a magnifying glass, but most need a **microscope**. That is why they are named *micro* — very small.

Try this: collect some moist soil, shake it in a beaker of water, let it settle and put a drop of the water on a glass slide under a microscope. You will see tiny moving organisms. Pond water shows even more.

Microbes live **everywhere** — in soil, water, air, inside our bodies and those of other animals. They survive in ice-cold Antarctica, in hot springs, in deserts and in marshes. Some live alone; others, like bacteria and some fungi, grow in **colonies** that become visible to the eye.

> Did you know? Your gut alone carries trillions of bacteria, many of which help you digest food.

Microorganisms are grouped into four major groups — **bacteria, fungi, protozoa and some algae** — plus **viruses**, which are quite different.

- **Bacteria** — single-celled, shaped like rods, spheres, spirals or commas. Example: *Lactobacillus* in curd.
- **Fungi** — bread mould (*Rhizopus*), *Penicillium*, *Aspergillus*, yeast, mushrooms (large fungi).
- **Protozoa** — single-celled animals such as *Amoeba* and *Paramecium*.
- **Algae** — *Chlamydomonas*, *Spirogyra*; they have chlorophyll and make food.
- **Viruses** — much smaller than bacteria. They **reproduce only inside the cells of a host** (bacteria, plant or animal). Outside a host they show no signs of life. Common cold, influenza, polio, chickenpox, measles and COVID-19 are caused by viruses.

Microbes may be **unicellular** (bacteria, many algae and protozoa) or **multicellular** (many algae and fungi).

check.why: Viruses have no life activity of their own; they multiply only after entering the cells of a host organism.

sections.h: Friendly microbes in the kitchen and the factory
sections.md:
**Making curd.** Milk contains a sugar called lactose. *Lactobacillus* bacteria multiply in warm milk and turn it into curd. They also help digestion. Curd is used in raita, lassi, dahi vada — and cheese, pickles and many foods are made using bacteria too.

**Baking and idli.** **Yeast** reproduces rapidly and gives off **carbon dioxide** during respiration. The gas bubbles fill the dough and make it rise — that is why bread, cakes and pastries are soft and spongy. Idli and dosa batter rises overnight for the same reason, through fermentation by microbes.

**Making alcohol and vinegar.** Yeast is used commercially to make alcohol from sugar, in a process called **fermentation**. Louis Pasteur discovered fermentation in 1857. Sugar syrup from barley, wheat, rice or crushed fruit is fermented by yeast to produce alcohol; acetic acid bacteria turn alcohol into vinegar.

**Medicines.** **Antibiotics** are medicines made from microorganisms that kill or stop the growth of disease-causing microbes. **Streptomycin, tetracycline and erythromycin** are examples. **Alexander Fleming** discovered **penicillin** in **1929** (published that year, after his 1928 observation) when he noticed that mould growing on a culture plate stopped bacteria growing around it.

Important: antibiotics work against **bacteria**, not viruses. They do not cure a cold or flu. Take them only when a qualified doctor prescribes them, and complete the full course. Misuse makes bacteria **resistant** and the medicine stops working. Antibiotics are also mixed in feed of livestock and used to control plant diseases.

When a disease-causing microbe enters our body, the body produces **antibodies** to fight it. The body also **remembers** how to fight that microbe if it enters again.

A **vaccine** contains dead or weakened microbes (or parts of them). When given to a healthy person, the body makes antibodies and remembers. If the real microbe attacks later, the body defeats it quickly. This is how vaccines protect against cholera, tuberculosis (BCG), smallpox, hepatitis, polio and measles.

**Edward Jenner** developed the vaccine for **smallpox in 1798**. Through worldwide vaccination, smallpox has been **eradicated** from the whole planet. India was declared **polio-free in 2014** after the Pulse Polio drive gave drops to crores of children.

Why do newborns get a vaccination card? Because the schedule protects them before they meet dangerous microbes.

check.q: Penicillin is an example of…
check.why: Penicillin is made by the mould Penicillium and kills or stops the growth of bacteria, which makes it an antibiotic.

sections.md:
**Increasing soil fertility.** Some bacteria and **blue-green algae** (cyanobacteria) **fix nitrogen** from the atmosphere, enriching soil with nitrogen compounds. These are called **biological nitrogen fixers**. *Rhizobium* lives in the root nodules of legumes such as peas and beans.

**Cleaning the environment.** Leaves, peels, dead animals and dung are broken down by microbes into simple substances that plants reuse. Try it: bury some peels and a polythene bag in two pots. After a month the peels have vanished into soil — the polythene has not. Microbes cannot break down plastic easily, which is why plastic waste is such a problem.

**The nitrogen cycle.** Our atmosphere is about **78% nitrogen**, but plants cannot use the gas directly.
1. Bacteria in soil and root nodules (and lightning) convert nitrogen into compounds.
2. Plants absorb these and make proteins.
3. Animals eat plants.
4. When plants and animals die, **decomposing bacteria and fungi** turn nitrogenous waste back into compounds.
5. Other bacteria convert some of these back to **nitrogen gas**, which returns to the air.

So the percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere stays more or less constant.

check.why: Some soil bacteria convert nitrogen compounds back into nitrogen gas, which keeps the atmospheric percentage roughly constant.

sections.md:
Microbes that cause disease are called **pathogens**. They enter our bodies through the air we breathe, the water we drink, the food we eat, or by direct contact with an infected person or carried by an animal.

**Communicable diseases** spread from an infected person to a healthy one through air, water, food or physical contact. Examples: cholera, common cold, chickenpox, tuberculosis. When someone with a cold sneezes, thousands of virus-filled droplets spray into the air — that's why we cover our mouth and nose.

**Carriers.** Some insects and animals carry pathogens. The **housefly** sits on garbage and then on uncovered food, transferring germs. The female **Anopheles mosquito** carries the malaria parasite (*Plasmodium*, a protozoan). The female **Aedes mosquito** carries the dengue virus. Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water — coolers, tyres, flower pots — so never let water collect.

check.why: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, carried by the female Anopheles mosquito.

sections.h: Diseases in animals and plants; food poisoning
sections.md:
**Animals:** **Anthrax** is a dangerous disease of humans and cattle caused by a bacterium; it was discovered by **Robert Koch in 1876**. **Foot-and-mouth disease** of cattle is caused by a virus.

**Plants:** microbes reduce crop yields. Citrus canker (bacteria, spread by air), rust of wheat (fungi, air and seeds), and yellow vein mosaic of bhindi (okra) (virus, carried by insects). Farmers control them with chemicals that kill the microbes.

**Food poisoning.** Some microbes growing on food produce **toxic substances**. Eating spoiled food can cause serious illness and even death. So preserving food properly matters a lot.

How do we keep food from spoiling? By stopping microbes from growing.

- **Chemical method:** **salt and edible oils** are common preservatives. **Sodium benzoate** and **sodium metabisulphite** are used in jams, squashes and pickles.
- **Preservation by salt:** meat, fish, raw mangoes, amla and tamarind are covered with dry salt — salt draws out water, and microbes cannot grow.
- **Sugar:** jams, jellies and squashes. Sugar reduces moisture.
- **Oil and vinegar:** pickles — bacteria cannot live in such an environment.
- **Heat and cold:** boiling kills many microbes; refrigerators slow their growth.
- **Pasteurisation:** milk is heated to about **70 °C for 15 to 30 seconds**, then suddenly chilled and stored. This kills harmful microbes. The method was discovered by **Louis Pasteur**.
- **Storage and packing:** dry fruits and vegetables are sold in sealed air-tight packets.

check.q: Why does a thick salt coating preserve raw mango?
options: Salt removes water, so microbes cannot grow
check.why: Salt draws water out of the food and out of microbes, so they cannot survive or multiply.

parts.md: Meera's grandmother never measured anything. Every night she warmed milk till it felt 'just warm on the wrist', stirred in a spoon of yesterday's curd, covered the pot and set it by the stove. One cold December night in Shimla, Meera did the same — but put the pot by the open window. In the morning the milk was still runny. 'Did I forget the magic?' she asked.

Her cousin Arjun, who had a school microscope, put a drop of grandmother's curd on a slide. Tiny rods swarmed across the field of view. 'These are Lactobacillus,' he said. 'They are alive. Cold slows them down; warmth lets them multiply.' They tried again — this time the pot sat wrapped in a shawl near the stove. By morning it had set, thick and tangy.

'So the bread uncle uses yeast the same way?' Meera asked. Arjun nodded. 'Yeast breathes out carbon dioxide. The bubbles puff up the dough.' Meera looked at her grandmother with new respect. She had been running a microbiology lab in the kitchen for fifty years without ever calling it that.

workedExamples.q: A bacterium divides into two every 20 minutes. Starting with one bacterium, how many will there be after 2 hours?
workedExamples.answer: 64 bacteria (which is why food left out spoils fast).

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch02-microorganis.title: Microorganisms: Friend and Foe — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch02-microorganis.subtitle: Where microbes live, curd and bread, medicines and vaccines, diseases, food preservation and the nitrogen cycle

sections.h: The five groups and where they live
sections.md:
Microorganisms (microbes) are too small to see with the naked eye; we use a **magnifying glass or microscope**. They fall into five main groups:

| Group | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bacteria | Lactobacillus, Rhizobium | Rod, spiral or round; single-celled |
| Fungi | Yeast, bread mould, Penicillium | Yeast single-celled; moulds form threads |
| Protozoa | Amoeba, Paramecium | Single-celled, often in water |
| Algae | Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra | Green, make their own food |
| Viruses | Cause cold, flu, polio, chickenpox | Reproduce only inside a host cell |

**Activity idea (as in the chapter):** take moist soil in a beaker of water, let it settle, and look at a drop under a microscope — you will see tiny moving organisms.

Microbes live **everywhere**: in ice-cold climates, hot springs, deserts, marshy land, soil, air, water, and inside our bodies. Some live alone (bacteria, yeast); some live in **colonies** (fungi, bacteria). Amoeba lives singly; fungi and bacteria can form groups visible to the eye.

check.q: Which microorganism can reproduce only inside the cells of a host?
check.why: Viruses have no machinery of their own to multiply, so they reproduce only inside living host cells.

sections.md:
**Making curd.** Add a spoonful of curd to warm milk. *Lactobacillus* bacteria in it multiply and turn milk into curd. Bacteria are also used for cheese, pickles and many foods. In idli and dosa batter, bacteria and yeast ferment the batter, making it rise.

**Baking.** **Yeast** respires and releases **carbon dioxide**; the gas bubbles fill the dough so bread, pastries and cakes become soft and spongy.

**Commercial use — fermentation.** Yeast grown on natural sugars in barley, wheat, rice and fruit juices converts sugar into **alcohol** (and CO₂). This conversion of sugar into alcohol is **fermentation**. **Louis Pasteur** discovered fermentation in 1857.

**Cleaning the environment.** Microbes decompose dead plants, animals and wastes into simple substances that other plants can use — the activity in the chapter: bury a pit with peels and leaves, and a plastic bag; after a month the peels are gone, the plastic remains.

sections.h: Microbes in medicine: antibiotics and vaccines
sections.md:
**Antibiotics** are medicines made from microorganisms that kill or stop the growth of disease-causing microbes. Examples: **streptomycin, tetracycline, erythromycin**. In **1929 Alexander Fleming** noticed that a mould, *Penicillium*, stopped the growth of bacteria in a culture plate — the discovery of **penicillin**. Antibiotics are also mixed with feed of livestock and poultry and used to control plant diseases.

Use antibiotics **only as prescribed by a qualified doctor**, and complete the course. They **do not work against viruses** like cold and flu; misuse makes bacteria resistant and can harm useful gut bacteria.

**Vaccines.** When a germ enters the body, the body makes **antibodies** to fight it and *remembers* it. A vaccine introduces **dead or weakened microbes**, so the body learns to fight without falling ill. Cholera, TB, smallpox and hepatitis are prevented by vaccines. **Edward Jenner** discovered the smallpox vaccine in **1798**. Smallpox has been eradicated worldwide; India's pulse polio campaign has made the country polio-free.

**Increasing soil fertility.** Some bacteria and blue-green algae **fix nitrogen** from the air into the soil — natural fertiliser.

check.q: Why should antibiotics not be taken for a common cold?
options: Colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill
check.why: Antibiotics act on bacteria, while the common cold is caused by a virus, so they do not help and can create resistance.

sections.h: Harmful microbes: diseases in humans, animals and plants
sections.md:
Disease-causing microbes are **pathogens**. They enter through air, water, food, contact, or carriers.

**Communicable diseases** spread from an infected person to a healthy one. A sneeze can carry thousands of virus particles — cover your nose and mouth.

**Carriers.** The housefly carries germs from garbage to food. Female *Anopheles* mosquito carries the malaria parasite (*Plasmodium*); female *Aedes* mosquito carries the dengue virus. Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water — so don't let water collect in coolers, tyres and pots.

| Human disease | Microbe | Spreads by | Prevention |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tuberculosis | Bacteria | Air | Isolate patient, BCG vaccine |
| Measles | Virus | Air | Vaccination |
| Chickenpox | Virus | Air/contact | Vaccination |
| Polio | Virus | Air/water | Vaccination |
| Cholera | Bacteria | Water/food | Hygiene, boiled water, vaccine |
| Typhoid | Bacteria | Water | Boiled water, vaccine |
| Hepatitis A | Virus | Water | Boiled water, vaccine |
| Malaria | Protozoan | Mosquito | Nets, repellents, no stagnant water |

**Animals:** anthrax (bacteria) in humans and cattle — discovered by **Robert Koch** in 1876; foot-and-mouth disease in cattle (virus).

**Plants:** citrus canker (bacteria, air), rust of wheat (fungi, air/seeds), yellow vein mosaic of bhindi (virus, insects). These reduce crop yield and are controlled by chemicals.

check.q: Which insect carries the malaria parasite?
check.why: The malaria parasite Plasmodium is carried from person to person by the female Anopheles mosquito.

sections.md:
Some microbes growing on food produce **toxins**; eating spoiled food causes **food poisoning**, which can be serious. Spoiled food smells bad, tastes odd and changes colour.

Methods of preservation:

- **Chemicals:** salt and edible oils; **sodium benzoate** and **sodium metabisulphite** are common preservatives in jams and squashes.
- **Common salt:** meat, fish, amla, raw mango, tamarind.
- **Sugar:** jams, jellies, squashes — sugar draws out moisture so bacteria can't grow.
- **Oil and vinegar:** pickles.
- **Heat and cold:** boiling milk kills many microbes; refrigerators slow their growth.
- **Pasteurisation:** milk heated to about **70°C for 15–30 seconds** and then suddenly chilled and stored — named after Pasteur.
- **Storage and packing:** airtight packets keep dry fruits and vegetables safe.

check.q: In pasteurisation, milk is…
options: heated to about 70°C for 15–30 seconds, then chilled quickly
check.why: Short heating to about 70°C followed by sudden chilling kills most microbes without spoiling the milk.

sections.md:
Air is about **78% nitrogen**, but plants and animals cannot use it directly. Certain bacteria and blue-green algae **fix** it into compounds; *Rhizobium* lives in the **root nodules of legumes** (peas, beans, gram). Lightning also fixes some nitrogen.

Plants absorb nitrogen compounds from soil to make **proteins**; animals get them by eating plants. When plants and animals die, **decomposer bacteria and fungi** convert the nitrogenous wastes back into compounds in the soil, and other bacteria release some as nitrogen gas into the air. So the percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere stays nearly constant.

rd-school-c8-science-a.ch03-coal-petrole.title: Coal and Petroleum
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch03-coal-petrole.subtitle: Sunlight trapped for 300 million years — and why we must not waste it

sections.md:
When your father kick-starts his scooter, he is burning sunlight that fell on Earth before the dinosaurs. That sounds like magic, but it is chemistry and geology. The petrol in the tank came from tiny sea organisms that captured the Sun's energy, died, sank, and were slowly cooked under rock for millions of years.

To understand this, we first sort the things nature gives us — **natural resources** — into two kinds.

**Inexhaustible natural resources** are present in unlimited quantity and are not likely to be used up by human activity: **sunlight, air**.

**Exhaustible natural resources** are limited in amount and can be exhausted by human activities: **forests, wildlife, minerals, coal, petroleum, natural gas**.

Some exhaustible resources like coal, petroleum and natural gas were formed from the dead remains of living organisms (fossils). So they are called **fossil fuels**.

> Did you know? Water is often listed as inexhaustible in total, but *clean fresh water* in a particular place can certainly run out — ask Chennai in the summer of 2019.

check.q: Which of these is an inexhaustible natural resource?
check.why: Sunlight is available in unlimited quantity and human use does not reduce it.

sections.h: Coal: how a forest turned to stone
sections.md:
Coal is as hard as stone and black in colour. It is one of the fuels used to cook food, and was once used in railway engines to produce steam. It is also used in **thermal power plants** to produce electricity and in industries.

**How was coal formed?** About **300 million years ago**, Earth had dense forests in low-lying wetland areas. Due to natural processes such as flooding, these forests got buried under the soil. As more soil deposited over them, they were compressed. The temperature also rose as they sank deeper and deeper. Under **high pressure and high temperature**, and in the absence of air, dead plants slowly converted to coal. As coal contains mainly **carbon**, this slow conversion of dead vegetation into coal is called **carbonisation**.

India has large coal deposits in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal — the Jharia and Raniganj fields are famous.

sections.md:
When heated in air, coal burns and produces mainly **carbon dioxide** gas. Industries process coal to get useful products:

- **Coke** — a tough, porous, black substance; an almost pure form of carbon. Used in the **manufacture of steel** and in extracting many metals.
- **Coal tar** — a black, thick liquid with an unpleasant smell. It is a mixture of about **200 substances**. Products from coal tar are used as starting materials for synthetic dyes, drugs, explosives, perfumes, plastics, paints, photographic materials and roofing materials. **Naphthalene balls** used to repel moths and insects come from coal tar. Roads were once surfaced with coal tar; today **bitumen**, a petroleum product, is mostly used.
- **Coal gas** — obtained during the processing of coal to get coke. It is used as a fuel in many industries near coal processing plants. It was first used for street lighting in **London in 1810** and in **New York around 1820**. Today, natural gas has largely replaced it.
keyTerms: Coke — nearly pure carbon, used for steel
Coal tar — thick black liquid, source of naphthalene
Coal gas — fuel gas from coal processing

check.q: Naphthalene balls are obtained from…
check.why: Naphthalene, used to keep moths away, is one of about 200 substances separated from coal tar.

sections.md:
Petrol runs cars and scooters; diesel runs trucks, buses, tractors, trains and generators. Both come from **petroleum** — from Latin *petra* (rock) and *oleum* (oil), because it is mined from between rocks.

**Formation:** petroleum was formed from organisms living in the **sea**. As these organisms died, their bodies settled at the bottom and got covered with layers of sand and clay. Over millions of years, absence of air, high temperature and high pressure transformed the dead organisms into **petroleum and natural gas**.

The layer containing petroleum oil and gas is above that of water, because oil and gas are lighter than water and do not mix with it. Drilling a well into such a trap brings up the oil.

The **world's first oil well** was drilled in Pennsylvania, USA, in **1859**. Eight years later, in **1867**, oil was struck at **Makum in Assam**. In India, petroleum is found in **Assam, Gujarat, Mumbai High** (offshore), and in the river basins of Godavari and Krishna. **Digboi** in Assam has one of the oldest working refineries in the world.

sections.h: Refining: one crude oil, many products
sections.md:
Petroleum straight from the well — **crude oil** — is a dark oily liquid with an unpleasant smell. It is a mixture of many constituents: petroleum gas, petrol, diesel, lubricating oil, paraffin wax and more. The process of separating these constituents (fractions) is called **refining**, and it is carried out in a **petroleum refinery**.

In a tall fractionating column, crude oil is heated. Lighter fractions rise higher and condense at cooler levels; heavier ones stay lower.

Many useful substances made from petroleum and natural gas are called **petrochemicals**: detergents, fibres (polyester, nylon, acrylic), polythene and other plastics. **Hydrogen gas** from natural gas is used to make fertilisers like urea. Because of its great commercial importance, petroleum is also called **'black gold'**.

sections.md:
**Natural gas** is a very important fossil fuel because it is easy to transport through pipes. It is stored under high pressure as **Compressed Natural Gas (CNG)**. CNG is used for power generation and increasingly as fuel for vehicles because it is a **less polluting fuel** — a cleaner fuel.

Delhi converted its buses and autorickshaws to CNG in the early 2000s after a Supreme Court order, and the city's air improved noticeably for a while. Natural gas reaches many homes directly through pipelines (PNG) in cities like Mumbai, Delhi and Ahmedabad.

India has natural gas reserves in **Tripura, Rajasthan, Maharashtra** and the **Krishna–Godavari delta**. Natural gas is also a starting material for many chemicals and fertilisers.

> Coal, petroleum and natural gas cannot be made in a laboratory from dead organisms — the process needs millions of years.

Fossil fuels are **limited**. They took millions of years to form and will be used up in a few hundred at our rate. Burning them also **pollutes air** and releases carbon dioxide, which is linked to **global warming**.

The **Petroleum Conservation Research Association (PCRA)** advises people on how to save petrol and diesel while driving:

- Drive at a constant and moderate speed as far as possible.
- **Switch off the engine** at traffic lights or wherever you have to wait.
- Ensure **correct tyre pressure**.
- Ensure **regular maintenance** of the vehicle.

And for all of us: walk or cycle short distances, use public transport, carpool, and use solar and wind energy where possible.

check.q: Which is NOT a PCRA tip to save fuel?
options: Switch off engine at red lights
check.why: Fast and uneven driving wastes fuel; PCRA recommends constant, moderate speed.

If 3 crore vehicles each idle 10 minutes a day, burning 0.01 L per minute of idling, how much fuel is wasted daily?
workedExamples.answer: 30 lakh litres a day — switching off at signals matters.

summary: Natural resources are inexhaustible (sunlight, air) or exhaustible (coal, petroleum, forests, minerals).
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels, formed from dead organisms over millions of years.
Coal formed about 300 million years ago from buried forests by carbonisation — heat, pressure, no air.
Coal products: coke (steel making), coal tar (dyes, drugs, naphthalene), coal gas (fuel).
Petroleum formed from dead sea organisms under sand and clay.
First oil well: Pennsylvania 1859; in India, Makum (Assam) 1867.
Refining separates crude oil into LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, paraffin wax, bitumen.
Petrochemicals give plastics, detergents, fibres and fertilisers; petroleum is 'black gold'.
CNG is a cleaner fuel transported by pipelines.
Fossil fuels are limited and polluting; PCRA tips help save fuel.
